extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, economists, and students of public finance and taxation
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and designing taxes (capitation, excise, customs, bounties) with attention to incidence, equity, administrative cost, and effects on labour, consumption, and smuggling. Grounded in classical political economy arguments and historical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitation taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitation taxes are levied at little expense; and, where they are rigorously exacted, afford a very sure revenue to the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cheap to collect and secure revenue when strictly enforced; common where comfort and security of inferior ranks are neglected; generally form only a small part of public revenue and could often be replaced by more convenient methods for the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes upon consumable commodities (indirect taxation of revenue)
rubrics_metrics.description: The state, not knowing how to tax directly and proportionably the revenue of its subjects, endeavours to tax it indirectly by taxing their expense, which, it is supposed, will, in most cases, be nearly in proportion to their revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxing consumption is used as a proxy for taxing income. The logic relies on the assumption that expense is generally proportional to revenue; practical design must consider what commodities are consumed and at what rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between necessaries and luxuries
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumable commodities are either necessaries or luxuries. Necessaries include not only those indispensably necessary for life but also whatever custom renders indecent for creditable people even of the lowest order to be without.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification depends on custom and decency as much as nature (examples: linen shirts, leather shoes as necessaries in some countries; beer, ale, wine as luxuries). Policy should use local custom-sensitive definitions when deciding which goods to tax or exempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of taxes on necessaries — wage-price pass-through (tax incidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tax upon the necessaries of life operates exactly in the same manner as a direct tax upon the wages of labour... the labourer cannot, for any considerable time, be said to advance it; it must always, in the long-run, be advanced to him by his immediate employer, in the advanced state of wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxes on necessaries raise their prices and thereby raise wages proportionally; employers and dealers shift the burden forward, producing overcharges that ultimately fall on consumers and landlords in various capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of taxes on luxuries — limited wage impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes upon what I call luxuries... will not necessarily occasion any rise in the wages of labour... Taxes upon luxuries are finally paid by the consumers of the commodities taxed, without any retribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Luxuries are paid by consumers across revenue types (wages, profits, rent); such taxes do not produce the same wage adjustments as taxes on necessaries and act more purely as consumer-level burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes on luxuries act as sumptuary laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The high price of such commodities does not necessarily diminish the ability of the inferior ranks of people to bring up families. Upon the sober and industrious poor, taxes upon such commodities act as sumptuary laws, and dispose them either to moderate, or to refrain altogether from the use of superfluities which they can no longer easily afford.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designing luxury taxes can deliberately reduce consumption (public-health or moral aims) and may even improve household provisioning among the sober poor; effects differ by social group and behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate overcharge through production chain (repetition of taxes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain taxes are, in the price of certain goods, sometimes repeated and accumulated four or five times... you must pay not only for the tax upon the leather of your own shoes, but for a part of that upon those of the shoemaker and the tanner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxes on necessaries can be compounded across inputs and services, magnifying final consumer prices; policy should account for cascading incidence when taxing inputs vs final goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation of staple necessaries (salt, leather, soap, candles)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Great Britain, the principal taxes upon the necessaries of life, are those upon... salt, leather, soap, and candles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heavy taxation on widely used staples raises subsistence costs and thus wages; governments may retain such taxes because they yield substantial revenue, but trade-offs with equity and economic distortion must be weighed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fuel/coal taxation affects industrial location and wages
rubrics_metrics.description: The price of fuel has so important an influence upon that of labour, that all over Great Britain, manufactures have confined themselves principally to the coal counties; other parts of the country, on account of the high price of this necessary article, not being able to work so cheap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxes on fuel/transportation of fuel (e.g., coastal carriage tax) significantly influence where manufacturing locates and the competitiveness of regions; exemptions or bounties on coal transport could be justified to reduce distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounties on exportation and prohibitions on importation produce bad effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The bounty upon the exportation of corn... produces all the like bad effects; and instead of affording any revenue, frequently occasions a very great expense to government. The high duties upon the importation of foreign corn... have all had the bad effects of taxes upon the necessaries of life, and produce no revenue to government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protectionist measures intended to favor domestic producers can increase prices for consumers and cost government revenue; reform requires public recognition of these futility and their adverse distributional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes that greatly raise prices may shrink revenue (excessive rates encourage smuggling or reduce consumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: High taxes, sometimes by diminishing the consumption of the taxed commodities, and sometimes by encouraging smuggling frequently afford a smaller revenue to government than what might be drawn from more moderate taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optimal taxation requires balancing rate vs compliance and demand elasticity; lowering rates can sometimes increase revenue by reducing smuggling and sustaining consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for revenue loss from smuggling: lower taxes or improve administration
rubrics_metrics.description: When the diminution of revenue is the effect of the encouragement given to smuggling, it may, perhaps, be remedied in two ways; either by diminishing the temptation to smuggle, or by increasing the difficulty of smuggling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy options: reduce tax differentials to lower smuggling incentives, or strengthen enforcement/administration (e.g., customs administration modeled on excise practices) to raise the cost of smuggling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two methods to tax consumables: licence (annual per consumer) vs dealer-stage taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumable commodities... may be taxed in two different ways. The consumer may either pay an annual sum on account of his using or consuming goods of a certain kind; or the goods may be taxed while they remain in the hands of the dealer...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice depends on durability of good (long-lasting goods better suited to licence), convenience for consumers (piece-meal payments), and administrative practicality; examples: coach-tax and plate tax (licence) vs excise/customs (dealer-stage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections to consumer-licence taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: The project... seems liable to the four following very important objections. First... more unequal. Secondly... would diminish piece-meal payment convenience. Thirdly... operate less as sumptuary laws. Fourthly... paying all at once might distress the workman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licences can be regressive or misaligned with actual consumption, reduce pay-as-you-go flexibility for the poor, blunt behavioral incentives, and impose liquidity burdens — important equity and behavioral considerations against flat licences for commonly consumed items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of excise: characteristics and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The duties of excise are imposed chiefly upon goods of home produce, destined for home consumption. They are imposed only upon a few sorts of goods of the most general use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excise duties are typically precise, limited in scope, and easier to define than customs duties; they usually fall on goods of general domestic consumption and can be administered with clarity about taxable goods and rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of customs: historical purpose and modern problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The duties of customs are much more ancient... They appear to have been originally considered as taxes upon the profits of merchants... In point of perspicuity, precision, and distinctness, therefore, the duties of customs are much inferior to those of excise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customs historically evolved from merchant profit taxation and include numerous specific rates and classifications (book of rates), producing uncertainty and classification disputes that impose administrative and compliance costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mercantile system uses taxes as monopoly instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: The taxes which at present subsist upon foreign manufactures... have, the greater part of them, been imposed for the purpose, not of revenue, but of monopoly, or to give our own merchants an advantage in the home market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When trade taxes aim to confer domestic monopoly rather than raise revenue, they often produce inefficiencies, encourage smuggling, and reduce overall national welfare; policy should distinguish revenue vs protection objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounties and drawbacks encourage fraud and reduce customs revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: The bounties which are sometimes given upon the exportation... and the drawbacks which are paid upon the re-exportation... have given occasion to many frauds, and to a species of smuggling, more destructive of the public revenue than any other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bounties/drawbacks create perverse incentives for fraudulent shipments and re-landing; they can create very large deductions from gross customs receipts and raise administrative expenses and enforcement challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification uncertainty in book of rates harms importers and officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The book of rates is extremely comprehensive... It is, upon this account, frequently uncertain under what article a particular sort of goods ought to be classed, and, consequently what duty they ought to pay. Mistakes... sometimes ruin the custom-house officer, and frequently occasion much trouble, expense, and vexation to the importer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customs schedules with many narrowly defined categories produce ambiguity and disputes; simpler, clearer classification systems improve fairness and reduce administrative risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative reform: adopt excise-like administration for customs / warehousing option
rubrics_metrics.description: By introducing into the customs a system of administration as similar to that of the excise as the nature of the different duties will admit, the difficulty of smuggling might be very much increased... The importer... might, at his option, be allowed either to carry them to his own private warehouse; or to lodge them in a warehouse... under the key of the custom-house officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms to reduce smuggling and disputes include harmonizing customs administration with excise practices (controls, records) and using secure warehousing under customs supervision to improve compliance and reduce incentives to smuggle.
